notes.bp: A listener must recognize Mandarin Tone 3 efficiently even when the voice has a creaky quality that changes the acoustic signal.
notes.wh: Tone, voice quality, and phonological context interact; a cue can make processing easier without being the tone itself.
notes.naive: Use pitch alone or treat creak as irrelevant speaker variation.
notes.ap: Test whether creaky voice changes the time and accuracy of Tone 3 processing, separating phonological benefit from general listening difficulty.
notes.mech: The paper studies how creaky voice facilitates more efficient phonological processing of Mandarin Tone 3.
notes.math: The speech cue is useful because it changes the listener's inference about a category boundary; processing efficiency is measured behaviorally rather than assumed from an acoustic correlation.
notes.ww: The paper reports behavioral evidence that creaky voice can facilitate Tone 3 processing in the tested Mandarin stimuli.
notes.limits: Listeners, stimuli, tone context, creak manipulation, and task bound the claim; a processing benefit is not a universal production or perception rule.
notes.title: Creaky Voice Facilitates More Efficient Phonological Processing of Mandarin Tone 3

notes.bp: Many Middle Eastern languages need speech recognition but have little transcribed data, tools, or standardized evaluation.
notes.wh: Language variety, script, dialect, speaker access, and scarce labels interact; multilingual transfer may help one variety while obscuring another.
notes.naive: Fine-tune a high-resource recognizer on a tiny sample and report one score without documenting the language or split.
notes.ap: Build and evaluate ASR resources for low-resourced Middle Eastern languages, making language-specific data and transfer limits explicit.
notes.mech: The paper studies automatic speech recognition for low-resourced Middle Eastern languages.
notes.math: Low-resource ASR is an infrastructure problem as well as a model problem: a documented corpus and baseline expose which errors come from missing data versus model choice.
notes.ww: The paper reports resources, baselines, and recognition results for the covered Middle Eastern languages.
notes.limits: Language selection, dialect, corpus size, transcription, speakers, and evaluation splits limit generalization across the region.
notes.title: Automatic Speech Recognition for Low-Resourced Middle Eastern Languages

notes.bp: In a triadic conversation, a person may look at one participant before taking a turn, and a turn-taking model should use that gaze rather than treating the group as one audio stream.
notes.wh: Three-way interaction creates competing addressees and overlapping cues; gaze timing can precede speech while being noisy or socially ambiguous.
notes.naive: Predict turn transitions from audio only or use one global gaze feature for the whole group.
notes.ap: Add person-specific gaze cues to multimodal turn-taking prediction and test whether they improve decisions in triadic conversations.
notes.mech: The paper studies gaze-enhanced multimodal turn-taking prediction in triadic conversations.
notes.math: Turn-taking is addressed to someone: person-conditioned visual cues resolve part of the interaction structure that an audio-only boundary cannot represent.
notes.ww: The paper reports turn-taking prediction results with gaze enhancement in triadic interaction.
notes.limits: Participants, camera setup, roles, task, gaze annotation, and latency bound generalization; gaze is a cue, not a deterministic intention signal.
notes.title: Gaze-Enhanced Multimodal Turn-Taking Prediction in Triadic Conversations

notes.bp: Speaker verification should protect voice representations so a system can compare speakers without exposing a reusable identity embedding.
notes.wh: Verification needs a useful similarity signal, but storing or transmitting speaker information creates privacy and attack risks.
notes.naive: Encrypt storage around an ordinary embedding or remove speaker information so verification becomes impossible.
notes.ap: Learn secure representations end to end and test the tradeoff between verification accuracy and privacy exposure.
notes.mech: The paper proposes privacy-preserving speaker verification via end-to-end secure representation learning.
notes.math: Privacy is built into the representation rather than added only at storage: the learned object should support the authorized comparison while limiting what an observer can recover.
notes.ww: The paper reports privacy and speaker-verification results for the proposed secure representation learning method.
notes.limits: Threat model, attacker access, datasets, privacy measure, calibration, and deployment protocol bound the claim; benchmark privacy is not a complete security proof.
notes.title: Privacy-Preserving Speaker Verification via End-to-End Secure Representation Learning

notes.bp: Editing a speech recording should change the requested words or sounds without inventing unrelated content or damaging the surrounding voice.
notes.wh: An editor must fill a gap using context, but a powerful generator can hallucinate plausible speech that is inconsistent with the speaker, timing, or meaning.
notes.naive: Regenerate the whole utterance or mask a span and trust unconstrained continuation.
notes.ap: Build a robust high-quality speech editor whose context use is constrained and evaluate whether edits remain faithful without hallucinations.
notes.mech: VoiceNoNG is a robust high-quality speech-editing model designed to avoid hallucinations.
notes.math: Editing is constrained completion: the model must change a local region while preserving identity, timing, and untouched context, so faithfulness is a separate target from audio quality.
notes.ww: The paper reports speech-editing quality and reduced hallucination behavior for the tested edits.
notes.limits: Edit type, context length, speaker set, alignment, metrics, and human judgments bound the claim; no-hallucination behavior is not guaranteed under arbitrary prompts.
notes.title: VoiceNoNG: Robust High-Quality Speech Editing Model without Hallucinations

notes.bp: A multilingual speech-translation system should serve many languages efficiently while preserving accuracy, rather than duplicating a full model for each direction.
notes.wh: Languages have different amounts of data and structures; sharing too much causes interference while separate modules waste parameters.
notes.naive: Use one monolithic model with uniform capacity or one model per language pair.
notes.ap: Use a parasitic dual-scale design that shares efficient global structure while preserving language-specific detail for multilingual speech translation.
notes.mech: The paper proposes novel parasitic dual-scale modeling for efficient and accurate multilingual speech translation.
notes.math: The model divides capacity by scale: shared computation handles reusable patterns, while finer or conditional structure protects language-specific translation behavior.
notes.ww: The paper reports multilingual translation accuracy and efficiency improvements for the tested language set.
notes.limits: Languages, directions, data imbalance, parameter budget, decoding, and metrics bound the result; efficiency on a benchmark is not equal quality for every language.
notes.title: Novel Parasitic Dual-Scale Modeling for Efficient and Accurate Multilingual Speech Translation

notes.bp: A zero-shot TTS system should imitate a target speaker while retrieving a speaking style that fits the requested expressive context.
notes.wh: Speaker identity and style are entangled; retrieving a style example can improve expressiveness but can also copy unwanted content or confuse whose voice is being produced.
notes.naive: Use one global style embedding or concatenate a reference clip without separating speaker and style information.
notes.ap: Use speaker-aware style retrieval-augmented generation so the system retrieves relevant style evidence while maintaining zero-shot speaker identity.
notes.mech: SA-RAS is a speaker-aware style retrieval-augmented method for expressive zero-shot TTS.
notes.math: Style retrieval is constrained by identity: the reference supplies how to speak, while the target speaker supplies who speaks, and generation must keep those roles distinct.
notes.ww: The paper reports expressive quality, speaker similarity, and style-control results for zero-shot synthesis.
notes.limits: Reference selection, speaker set, style labels, prompts, listening tests, and language bound the claim; style similarity is not a complete account of naturalness.
notes.title: SA-RAS: Speaker-Aware Style Retrieval Augmented Generation for Expressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis

notes.bp: A human-like avatar's beat gesture can change how listeners understand or attend to speech, so gesture is part of the communicative signal rather than decoration.
notes.wh: Perception combines timing, visual form, speech content, and expectations about an avatar; a gesture can help one phrase and distract in another.
notes.naive: Add random gestures or assume a visually human avatar automatically improves speech perception.
notes.ap: Manipulate beat gestures made by human-like avatars and measure their effect on speech perception under controlled conditions.
notes.mech: The paper studies how beat gestures made by human-like avatars affect speech perception.
notes.math: Gesture functions as timed emphasis: its effect depends on alignment with prosodic or semantic structure, so perception experiments are needed instead of a visual-quality proxy.
notes.ww: The paper reports speech-perception effects of avatar beat gestures in the tested stimuli and listener tasks.
notes.limits: Avatar design, gesture timing, speech material, participants, and task bound generalization; a laboratory effect is not proof of conversational benefit.
notes.title: Beat gestures made by human-like avatars affect speech perception
